answer: In urban habitats in the Barcelona province, urban land use promoted invasion via the Gardening pathway—i.e., the establishment of ornamental woody (shrub/tree) and perennial herbaceous plants that escaped from gardens. Urban habitat plots had a 5.9-fold higher rate of Gardening-pathway species (IRR = 5.94, 95% CI: 1.97–17.90, p = 0.0015; n = 632 plots, 65 urban, 567 non-urban) compared to other habitats. Gardening-pathway species were disproportionately woody (47.6% shrub/tree) and perennial (42.9%) relative to other pathways (Fisher's exact OR = 4.16 for shrub/tree, p = 0.005; OR = 0.10 for annual, p = 0.0001), consistent with the ornamental-plant escape mechanism. This pattern coincides with the dramatic rise in Gardening-pathway introductions since 1985 (75.2% of all introductions in 1985–2019 vs. 16.8% before 1500; χ² = 230.4, df = 6, p < 10⁻⁴⁷), reflecting the expansion of urban land use in the region. In peri-urban areas (non-urban plots with urban land use in the 50 m buffer), urban land use also significantly increased the probability of Unintentional-pathway invasion (OR = 7.88, 95% CI: 1.30–47.86, p = 0.025), suggesting that urbanization facilitates both ornamental escape and accidental introduction of non-native plants.

payload.workflow: 1) Poisson GLM of pathway-specific species counts (n.gard, n.unint, n.agfo) on urban land cover (50 m buffer, 2009), habitat, elevation, and distance to road (n = 632 plots); simplified and sensitivity models (± progressive change, ± habitat) for robustness. 2) Fisher's exact tests on pathway × growth form (n = 81 species). 3) Chi-square test on 4×3 temporal contingency table of introduction pathways. 4) Peri-urban logistic regression on non-urban plots (n = 567).
